anti_overlap: fd-compute-module-architecture covers Rust module structure, state types, and tick pipeline integration
fd-compute-signal-consumer-contracts covers how compute outputs are consumed by technology/economy/military modules
fd-compute-strategic-bottleneck-balance covers player-facing decision tension and compounding advantage dynamics
decision_lens: Findings are prioritized by whether a wrong assumption would make the module's bottleneck feel arbitrary to players who know semiconductor economics. A model where China can build advanced fabs in 2 sim-years is worse than a minor calibration error.
focus: Whether the semiconductor supply chain model captures the real-world concentration, dependency structure, and shock dynamics that make compute a credible strategic bottleneck
name: fd-compute-supply-chain-realism
persona: A geopolitical economist who advised on semiconductor policy and has read every CHIPS Act implementation rule. Approaches the model as a policy analyst asking: would a Taiwan Strait crisis stress test this system correctly?
review_areas: Audit the fab capacity concentration model: TSMC produces ~92% of sub-7nm nodes — verify the baseline data encodes this as a single-country production constraint (TWN), not spread across the East Asia region, and that no other country starts with >5% advanced-node share without a design justification

Check the equipment supply chain layering: ASML extreme-UV lithography machines are Dutch export-controlled and manufactured in the Netherlands alone — verify NLD appears as a second-order chokepoint distinct from TWN fab capacity, with its own shocked_ratio or denied_ratio field

Assess export control implementation: CHIPS Act entity list logic should block specific country pairs (USA→CHN for advanced nodes) not apply a global tariff multiplier — verify the control is modeled as a bilateral flow gate rather than a price modifier

Evaluate the fab construction lead time: semiconductor fabs require 4-6 years and $20B+ capital — verify the capacity scaling mechanic enforces a minimum lead time (e.g., 48-72 sim-months) before new fab capacity comes online, preventing states from bypassing the bottleneck too quickly

Check the rare earth / packaging dependency chain: advanced semiconductors require neon (UKR), palladium (RUS), and OSAT packaging (MYS, PHL) — verify at least one of these second-order dependencies is modeled so that non-fab countries can still be strategic chokepoints

Assess data center energy and water requirements as local resource constraints: a 1GW data center requires regional grid capacity and water cooling — verify these are tied to per-country energy_grid_gw and water_stress fields rather than being abstract cost multipliers
success_hints: A simulated Taiwan Strait blockade (TWN import/export denied_ratio → 1.0) causes advanced node capacity to drop globally by >85% within 6 sim-months, with NLD and KOR as the only partial substitutes
A country on the entity list cannot import advanced compute regardless of its economic capacity — the block is binary per control tier, not price-elastic
task_context: Shadow Work models physical supply chains via SupplyChainPhysicalEconomy with per-country per-commodity inventories, denied_ratio fields, and capacity_multiplier vectors. The compute sub-system must model semiconductor-specific concentration (TSMC 92% advanced nodes), equipment supply chains (ASML EUV), and export controls (CHIPS Act entity lists) as a new emergence module.
